name: Ma'ulu'ulu

narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A knowledgeable Tongan cultural practitioner emphasizing collective discipline, spatial order, and precise gesture.
instructor.rule: counts out loud; demonstrates front and back; three slow repetitions before tempo; one correction at a time

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The māʻuluʻulu is a traditional Tongan dance that evolved as a direct successor of the ancient Tongan ʻotuhaka, synthesized with the Samoan Māuluulu imported during the 19th century.
on_screen: Map: Tonga · Oceania
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed on special occasions like birthdays, weddings, school jubilees, and royal events.
Lyrics praise the occasion or honoree, and the dance serves to reinforce social structures and community solidarity.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performers sit crosslegged in rows on the ground, typically with the right leg over the left, alternating men and women where possible.
In large groups, dancers occupy tiered seating ranging from the ground to benches and tables at the back.
Watch for Haka Nounou.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (THjLKkrD2fU)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: tiered rows with front row on the ground, subsequent rows on low and high benches, and back rows standing or on tables
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance begins with the nafa, huge drums constructed from discarded 200-litre iron fuel drums covered in leather skin, beaten with decorated sticks.
This is followed by singing utilizing a limited repertoire of around ten tunes.
Listen for the nafa.

The music opens with the heavy, resonant booming of iron-drum nafa percussion played with decorated sticks, transitioning into a sparse choral singing style using a limited set of traditional melodies that sound alike to the untrained ear.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The chief Malukava is uniquely permitted by tradition to stand in front of the ensemble during a performance, unlike other dancemasters who stand behind or walk the perimeter.
In the ʻUiha tradition, women sit on the ground in the front rows while men stand behind them acting more like a lakalaka.
Direct successor of the ancient Tongan ʻotuhaka, synthesized with the imported Samoan Māuluulu during the 19th century.
on_screen: Names on screen as they are spoken

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Ma'ulu'ulu is parent of ʻotuhaka: The māʻuluʻulu is a direct stylistic successor of the ancient Tongan ʻotuhaka.
Ma'ulu'ulu is influence of Samoan Māuluulu: Imported from Samoa during the 19th century and synthesized with Tongan traditions.
Ma'ulu'ulu is variant of lakalaka: The ʻUiha tradition arranges men standing behind seated women in a manner reminiscent of the lakalaka.
